 name: Release
 
 # Publishing a GitHub Release (which creates the tag, e.g. `v0.1.1`) builds and
 # publishes every artifact — the Rust crates to crates.io and the Java libraries
 # to Maven Central (with the renderer's native libraries for every supported
 # platform) — then attaches the built files to the Release.
 #
 # The tag drives the version: the workflow writes the tag's `X.Y.Z` into the Rust
 # workspace version and the Java parent version (in CI only) before building, and
 # a `bump` job commits that version back to `main` afterwards. No pre-bump commit
 # is required. Tags must be `v<major>.<minor>.<patch>` (an optional pre-release
 # suffix is allowed).
 #
 # The publish steps are idempotent, so re-running a partially failed release is
 # safe (a crate+version already on crates.io is skipped; Maven Central rejects a
 # re-deploy of an existing version).
 #
 # Secrets:
 #   CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN  crates.io API token (publish scope)
 #   GPG_PRIVATE_KEY       armored GPG private key (signing)
 #   GPG_PASSPHRASE        its passphrase
 #   CENTRAL_USERNAME      Sonatype Central Portal user token username
 #   CENTRAL_PASSWORD      Sonatype Central Portal user token password
 
 on:
   release:
     types: [published]
   workflow_dispatch:
     inputs:
       tag:
         description: 'Tag to release (e.g. v0.1.1); blank = current ref'
         required: false
 
 permissions:
   contents: write
 
 jobs:
   version:
     name: Resolve + validate version
     runs-on: ubuntu-latest
     outputs:
       tag: ${{ steps.v.outputs.tag }}
       version: ${{ steps.v.outputs.version }}
     steps:
       - id: v
         name: Derive the version from the tag
         run: |
           set -euo pipefail
           tag="${{ github.event.release.tag_name || inputs.tag || github.ref_name }}"
           if [[ ! "$tag" =~ ^v[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+(-[0-9A-Za-z.-]+)?$ ]]; then
             echo "::error::tag '$tag' must be v<major>.<minor>.<patch>"
             exit 1
           fi
           version="${tag#v}"
           echo "tag=$tag version=$version"
           echo "tag=$tag" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
           echo "version=$version" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
 
   rust:
     name: Publish crates to crates.io
     runs-on: ubuntu-latest
     needs: version
     steps:
       - uses: actions/checkout@v4
         with:
           ref: ${{ needs.version.outputs.tag }}
       - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable
 
       - name: Set the version from the tag
         working-directory: lib/rust
         run: |
           set -euo pipefail
           cargo install cargo-edit --locked
           cargo set-version --workspace "${{ needs.version.outputs.version }}"
           # Sanity: the workspace version + the intra-workspace path-dep pins.
           awk -F'"' '/^version = /{print "workspace:", $2; exit}' Cargo.toml
           grep -rho 'pathland-[a-z-]*", version = "[^"]*"' crates/*/Cargo.toml | sort -u
 
       - name: Test the publishable crates
         working-directory: lib/rust
         run: cargo test -p pathland-core -p pathland-engine -p pathland-view -p pathland-core-transport -p pathland-render-html
 
       - name: Publish in dependency order
         working-directory: lib/rust
         env:
           CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN }}
         run: |
           set -euo pipefail
           version="${{ needs.version.outputs.version }}"
           crates=(pathland-core pathland-engine pathland-view pathland-core-transport pathland-render-html)
           for c in "${crates[@]}"; do
             echo "::group::publish $c $version"
             # Idempotent: skip a crate+version already on crates.io.
             if curl -sf -A "pathland-release-ci" "https://crates.io/api/v1/crates/$c/$version" >/dev/null; then
               echo "$c $version already published — skipping"
               echo "::endgroup::"
               continue
             fi

             # `--allow-dirty`: `cargo set-version` above intentionally edits the
             # crates' manifests (the path-dep version pins), so the tree is "dirty".
             cargo publish --allow-dirty -p "$c"
             echo "::endgroup::"
             # Let the index propagate so the next dependent crate resolves it.

       - name: Package (guarantee .crate files for the release assets)
         working-directory: lib/rust
         run: |
           set -euo pipefail
           # All dependencies are published by now, so packaging every crate works.
           for c in pathland-core pathland-engine pathland-view pathland-core-transport pathland-render-html; do
             cargo package --allow-dirty -p "$c"
           done
 
       - name: Upload the .crate files
         uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
         with:
           name: crates
           path: lib/rust/target/package/*.crate
           if-no-files-found: error

     runs-on: ${{ matrix.runner }}
     needs: version

       fail-fast: false

           - { platform: windows-x86_64, runner: windows-latest }
           - { platform: linux-x86_64, runner: ubuntu-latest }
           - { platform: linux-aarch64, runner: ubuntu-24.04-arm }
           - { platform: macos-aarch64, runner: macos-14 }

 # Pathland Project - AI Agent Guide
 
 This document provides essential context for AI agents (or human contributors) working on the **Pathland** protocol. It captures the project's direction, architectural decisions, and implementation details to ensure consistency.
 
 **Last Updated**: November 1, 2026
 
 ---
 
 ## Architecture: Rust Opcode Engine
 
 > The canonical core is a **Rust engine** that emits the application's
 > **declarative view structure** — VStack, HStack, Text, spacing, padding,
 > alignment — as a fixed **16-byte opcode ring buffer** into shared linear
 > memory, consumed by host renderers. View components and modifiers are written
 > in Rust with a SwiftUI-like API, and in Java with the hand-written
 > **`dev.pathland.view` DSL** (reusable library, Java 17+); both drive the engine
 > through the flat **native C ABI** (`pathland-view-native`) over a zero-copy shared
 > ring on desktop.
 
 ### The 16-byte Opcode Engine
 
 - Every opcode is exactly **16 bytes**: `Category (1B) | Command ID (1B) | Flags (2B) | A (4B) | B (4B) | C (4B)`, `#[repr(C, packed)]`, little-endian.
 - A 64-byte cache line holds exactly **4 opcodes** → L1-cache-friendly.
 - Opcodes live in a **ring buffer** in linear memory; the guest writes at `writeCursor`, the host reads from `readCursor`; frame boundaries via a monotonic `frameCount` in the header block.
 - **Both directions are binary**: a second **event ring** (host → guest) carries `EVENT`-category opcodes. The renderer writes raw inputs at `eventWriteCursor`; the guest drains them at `eventReadCursor`. Events are 16-byte opcodes through the engine, never a side-channel callback.
 - **Variable-length data** (strings, token paths) lives in a bump **arena**; opcodes reference entries by offset (`[u32 byteLength][bytes...]`), so every opcode stays 16 bytes. A second host-owned **event arena** mirrors this in the host → guest direction (shared-memory event strings, e.g. `TEXT_CHANGED`); over the network, host → guest strings ride the batch's string section.
 - **Window metadata** (`META::SET_WINDOW_METADATA`, field family `TITLE`/`DESCRIPTION`/`LOCALE`) carries the hosting surface's presentation metadata; renderers map it to their own chrome (browser `<title>`/meta description/`<html lang>`, GTK/Qt window title). It is root-scoped and signal-backed, so a route title is a computed over the router. Web-only artifacts (canonical/robots/sitemap) stay host-owned.
 - Spec: **`spec/OPCODE.md`** (primary) + **`spec/CONFORMANCE.md`** (golden vectors). Companion catalogs: **`spec/PRIMITIVES.md`** (views), **`spec/MODIFIERS.md`** (modifiers/properties), **`spec/EVENTS.md`** (events), **`spec/LAYOUT.md`** (frame & layout allocation contract) — draft IDs are allocated there spec-first.
 
 ### Declarative, not positioned (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
 
 > **The engine describes WHAT the UI is — VStack, HStack, Text, spacing,
 > padding, alignment — never WHERE it is. It does not compute layout and does
 > not emit rects.**
 
 - The engine emits **declarative structure** (`TREE` create/delete/insert/remove/move) + **constraint properties** (`PARAMETER` spacing/padding/alignment/FILL/HUG hints).
 - **Native elements everywhere**: each platform's renderer maps the opcode stream onto that platform's native elements — GTK4 widgets on desktop, DOM elements in the browser, HTML server-side — and those native elements lay themselves out. Never a generic canvas unless a platform has no native equivalent.
 - **Reactive emission**: emission is diff-based. Only the nodes that changed emit opcodes (property diffs via `SET_PROPERTY`/`SET_TEXT`, structural diffs via `TREE` opcodes). An unchanged tree emits **zero** opcodes. Signals in the application mark the tree dirty; the engine reconciles.
 - **Zero dynamic heap allocations** during steady-state emission (proven by test).
 
 ### no_std / wasm32 direction guard (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
 
 `pathland-core` and `pathland-view` must remain `#![no_std]` + `alloc` and
 compile for `wasm32-unknown-unknown`. This is the guarantee that the protocol
 core can still target a browser / embedded / remote projection later (goal #15,
 Quarkus SSR + WebSocket). The desktop path (`pathland-view-native`) is the only
 consumer today, but the core must not become desktop-only. Verify with
 `lib/rust/check-wasm.sh` (i.e. `cargo build -p pathland-core -p pathland-view
 --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`).
 
 ### Reactive signals (Angular-style)
 
 `pathland-core::signal` provides writable signals that live in the engine. A
 node binds its text (`Node::text_binding`), a property
 (`Node::property_bindings`) or a **string property** (`Node::string_bindings`,
 e.g. a media controller's `MEDIA_SOURCE`) to a `SignalId`; during emit the engine
 resolves the binding and records the dependency, and `Engine::set_signal`
 re-emits **only the bound nodes** (`SET_TEXT` / `SET_PROPERTY`) — no full tree
 walk. Signal values
 are one of `F32`/`U32`/`Bool`/`Enum`/`Str` (packed to the wire's `u32` value or
 arena string). Foreign hosts reach signals via the flat C ABI
 (`pathland_native_signal_create_*` / `signal_set_*` / `node_bind_text` /
 `node_bind_property`) and the Java `Signal` type. Binding then calling `emit`
 records the dependency; a subsequent `set` is a partial emit. (Computed/derived
 signals + effects are the planned next step.)

 ```

   (`render_document_linked`, C ABI `pathland_html_render_linked` +
   `pathland_html_base_css[_name]`, Java `renderLinked`/`baseCss`/`baseCssName`)
   emits `{base}/base-<hash>.css`. The Spring Boot and Quarkus starters use it
   and serve the renderer-owned bytes immutable (global + mounted bases); token
   overrides/fit rules stay inline.
 - `scripts/lib.sh` (`build_rust_html`), the Maven `refresh-ide` profile, and CI
   run the design build + sync. Do not edit generated CSS by hand.
 
 ### Native C-ABI shim (`pathland-view-native` + `pathland-core-capi`)
 
 The **desktop/cross-language zero-copy path**: `pathland-view-native` exposes the
 flat world (the flat `builder`/`engine` surface) as `pathland_native_*` C
 functions with a **shared-memory ring** the host driver reads in place. Any
 language that links the dylib (Swift/Java/C# via FFI) calls the flat surface —
 no per-component wrappers — and consumes opcodes zero-copy.
 
 `pathland-core-capi` (`libpathland_core`) is the **minimal ring C ABI** for the
 Java DSL: `pathland_core_create`/`destroy`, `pathland_ring_buffer_push` (one
 raw 16-byte opcode), `pathland_core_arena_alloc`, frame boundaries, zero-copy
 `ring_ptr`/`ring_len`, and event drain/send. The Java DSL
 (`dev.pathland.view.core.ffm`) binds it with **JNA** (lazily loaded, zero JNI) and
 owns the retained tree + diff emission itself.
 
 ### GTK4 Renderer (`pathland-render-gtk`)
 
 The desktop renderer: a single crate that owns **all** GTK/glib/pango usage and
 maps opcode frames **incrementally** onto native GTK widgets (a retained
 `id → gtk::Widget` map). Both the Rust demo and the Java demo render through
 it — the demos **never call GTK or Swing directly**:
 
 - Rust demo links `pathland-render-gtk` as an `rlib` and calls `GtkRenderer::run(...)`
   with a wake closure.
 - Java demo (`pathland-gtk-demo`) loads `pathland-render-gtk` as a `cdylib` via JNA and
   calls `pathland_gtk_run_ring(ring, on_event, width, height)` over the Java DSL's own
   `libpathland_core` ring; native inputs round-trip as `EVENT` opcodes through the shared
   ring. The renderer **writes** the events and **wakes** the host (no payload); the host
   drains the event ring itself via `pathland_core_drain_events`. Events are never
   delivered through a side-channel callback — they flow through the opcode engine.
   The demo mounts `MusicPlayerView` (the same shared views the web demos use) with the
   app-driven media contract: the renderer plays the tracks through a direct GStreamer
   `playbin` and reports `MEDIA_*` events back; the demo's web-style
   `/_pathland/assets/...` paths resolve against an extracted local asset root
   (`pathland_gtk_set_asset_root`).
 
 The renderer maps native inputs onto the raw `Event` surface via GTK4
 controllers (`Button::clicked` → pointer up, `EventControllerMotion` →
 pointer move/enter/leave), emitting events through the same `Pump::send_input`
 path.
 
 `pathland_gtk::run` passes an explicit empty argv to GTK (the process command
 line belongs to the embedding host — e.g. the JVM's `-cp`/`-D` flags — and must
 not be parsed as GTK options).
 
 ### Native Java DSL (`dev.pathland.view`, in `lib/java/pathland-view`)
 
 The **hand-written, zero-dependency Java 17+ DSL** (no codegen). It is the
 SwiftUI-like authoring surface shared by desktop, Spring Boot, and Quarkus
 apps. Components and modifiers:
 
 - `View` is an **open interface** — the library ships `Text`/`Image`/`Color`/
   `Rectangle`, `VStack`/`HStack`/`ZStack`, `Spacer`, `Button`,
   `TextField(placeholder, WritableSignal<String>)`, `Video` (a
   `MediaController`'s surface), and application code (Quarkus/Spring/desktop)
   defines its own views by implementing `View`. **Media is a state object, not a
   view** (spec/MEDIA.md): `MediaController` owns the resource + transport as
   signals, a `Video` surface renders it, and **audio has no view** — the app
   binds its own buttons/sliders (`controller.attach()` materializes the
   controller's node once, outside any swapping branch, so a band swap never
   restarts playback).
 - **Custom views and styles use the configurator** (spec DSL.md §2): an
   app-authored `View` with values implements `Configurable<View.Config>`, holds a
   **`private` constructor**, and exposes
   `static ViewBuilder<View, Config> make(Consumer<Config>)`; a style
   (`ButtonStyle`/`LabelStyle`/`VideoStyle`) expose a
   **lowercase static factory** on their own type returning the style value
   (`BorderedButtonStyle.borderedButtonStyle(s -> s…)`), mirroring the library's
   `Modifiers.*` lowercase functions (e.g.
   `borderedButtonStyle(b -> b.padding(..).background(..)…)`). Creation goes
   through the configurator, never a parameterized constructor. The
   `pathland-view-processor` `ViewAuthoringProcessor` **errors** on
   public/protected constructors **with parameters** in custom `View` **and**
   `Style` implementations (no-arg roots and abstract types are exempt), so the
   convention is compile-enforced where the processor is wired
   (`annotationProcessorPaths`). The library's own views/styles follow the same
   shape (`Video`, `Text`, `BorderedButtonStyle`, …).
 - **SwiftUI-style `body()` / reactive components**: composite views declare
   `View body()` (their subtree); the library's primitives override
   `renderNode(Environment)` to materialize a `PathlandNode` (`render(Environment)` is
   the emitter entry point and must not be overridden). `body()` is a **tracked
   render function**: a signal read there subscribes that component, and a later
   write re-renders only that component and diffs its retained subtree — so plain
   `if`/`switch`/`for` over signals works. A signal **bound** to a node
   (`Text.make(t -> t.text(Signal))`) stays fine-grained and does not re-run the
   body. Non-signal reads are mount-time only; render bodies must be pure/idempotent
   and must not write signals. Each child view is a component slot; the root chain
   (body delegation, modifiers, environment/tap/navigation wrappers) is one slot.
   `View.of(Supplier<View>)` is the inline form (Java has no `if` expression);
   `ForEach.of(list | Signal<List<T>>, (item, index) -> View)` is the reactive
   list component (static lists may use streams/`for` directly).
   `NavigationContainer` / `SizeThatFits` are ordinary components. The root
   component type must stay stable across re-renders. (Rust parity is Phase 2.)
 - **Cross-language vocabulary** (spec DSL.md §9.3.1): the same anchors across
   Swift, Java, Kotlin, Rust, and TypeScript — `View`, `body`/`build`, `Signal`,
   `computed`, `State`, `ForEach`, `View.of`, `children`, `modifiers`. Use native
   control flow (`if`/`switch` in Swift/Java, `if`/`when` in Kotlin, `if`/`match`
   in Rust, ternary/`switch` in TypeScript); Java uses `View.of` only where an
   inline expression is needed. Swift is the canonical SwiftUI-shaped reference;
   Kotlin is implemented by `lib/java/pathland-view-kotlin` (Kotlin-owned views and
   modifiers over `pathland-view-core`), Swift is not implemented yet, and Rust
   parity is Phase 2.
 - **The three operations (spec DSL.md §2)**: every concrete view exposes
   `make(...)` (values — the only static; `make(Consumer<Config>)`, `make(value)`,
   `make()`), and the instance operations `.modifiers(ViewModifier...)` and
   `.children(View...)` chain on the returned builder. Java's static-vs-instance
   rule means the statics sit on the view class, the chain on the builder; a bare
   `View` value applies modifiers through the interface default
   `View.modifiers(...)`. Values are a
   fluent per-view `Config` (`VStack.make(v -> v.alignment(...).spacing(8))`,
   `Text.make(t -> t.text("hi"))`); modifiers are `ViewModifier` values built by
   the **`Modifiers` facade's lowercase functions** — one
   `import static dev.pathland.view.Modifiers.*;` brings the whole modifier
   vocabulary (`padding(p -> p.uniform(16))`, `frame(f -> f.width(100))`,
   `borderedButtonStyle(b -> …)`) — or, for single values, the value itself
   (`FontWeight.BOLD`, `Font.headline()`, a `ButtonStyle`). The `View` interface has
   **no per-modifier sugar** (`font`/`navigate`/`environment`/`onPathChange` were
   removed — use `.modifiers(Font…)`, `.modifiers(NavigationIntent.navigate(…))`,
   `.modifiers(environmentBinding(e -> e.key(…).value(…)))`,
   `.modifiers(pathChange(p -> p.listener(…)))`), and the `*Mod` shims
   (`EnvironmentMod`→`EnvironmentBinding`, `router/NavigationMod`→`NavigationIntent`,
   `PathChangeMod`→`PathChange`, `FontWeightMod`→`FontWeight`, …) are **removed**.
 - **Single-value shortcuts (spec DSL.md §2)**: a view/modifier whose config has a
   designated primary member also exposes a single-value construction overload that
   is pure sugar for the lambda — views construct with `make(value)` / `make(Signal<T>)`
   (`Text.make("hi")`), modifiers with the lowercase function's value form
   (`padding(16)`, `fontSize(sizeSignal)`). Multi-member configs (`Padding.edges`, `Offset`,
   `Gauge`, `Border`, …) have **no** shortcut — use the lambda. The shortcut delegates
   to the same `make(Consumer<Config>)` (views) / `Modifiers` facade
   (modifiers) factory via the package-private
   `Configurators` helper (one construction path). The former `.of(...)` construction
   factories are **removed** — a shortcut (or the lambda / `.children(...)` / empty
   `make()` for config-less views) replaces every one. Only data/branch factories keep
   `of`: `Color.of/rgb/argb/token`, `Fit.of`, `View.of`, `ForEach.of`,
   `EnvironmentKey.of`, `Route.of`, `Params.of`, `Signals.*`.
   Sizing is the `Frame` modifier value
   (`frame(f -> f.width(w).height(h).alignment(..))` and the lambda
   configurator `frame(f -> f.minWidth(..).maxWidth(..).alignment(..))`
   (min/ideal/max bounds)); all
   compile to the same `WIDTH`/`HEIGHT`/`ALIGNMENT`/min-max `SET_PROPERTY`s.
   Typed enums
   (`Alignment`/`TextAlignment`/`FontWeight`/`Truncation`), not raw ints.
 - **Environment scoping via a `ThreadLocal`** (Java 17+): a `ButtonStyle` modifier
   injects a style down the whole child tree; `ButtonStyle.makeBody(Configuration)`
   with built-in `PlainButtonStyle` / `BorderedButtonStyle`. Custom wrappers via
   `ViewModifier.body(View)`. The `Environment` also carries the session's
   `PersistentState`.
 - **Reactivity (Angular parity)** in `dev.pathland.view.core.signal`:
   `Signals.signal/computed/effect/untracked` — lazy+memoized computeds,
   glitch-free synchronous flush, equality suppression, error caching, write
   discipline (`allowWrites()`), circular-dependency detection.
 - **Persisted view state** (`dev.pathland.view.core.state`): a `State<T>` field (e.g.
   `State<Integer> count = new State<>(0);`) is auto-wired to the session's
   `PersistentState` (keyed by field name, or `new State<>(0, "key")` for an explicit
   key) by the `pathland-view-processor` annotation processor, which detects `State`
   fields by type and generates a `<View>_StateBinder` per view class. Each view
   connects its own `State` when it renders (`View.render` calls `Environment.state()
   → PersistentState.connect(view)`), so nested views can be instantiated inline in
   `body()` and need not be declared as fields. `PersistentState.signal(name, initial)`
   auto-loads the persisted value and auto-saves on change (key `name:scope`), and
   `StateStore` is untyped (one store serves all signal types).
 - **Fine-grained emitter** (`dev.pathland.view.engine`): mounts a view tree once,
   assigns stable ids, and registers a **node-level binding effect** per reactive
   text/property — a signal change re-emits only that node's `SET_TEXT` /
   `SET_PROPERTY` (unchanged signals emit zero opcodes). Sinks: `FrameOpcodeSink`
   (self-contained frames for SSR/WebSocket) and `RingOpcodeSink` (JNA into
   `libpathland_core`). The wire codec (`dev.pathland.view.core.transport`) mirrors
   `pathland_core_transport` (`PLPL` batch format, self-contained frames + events).
 
 Consistency with `pathland_core::constants` is enforced by the emitter/HTML
 tests (golden byte layout + round-trips), replacing the old codegen assert pass.
 
 - **Single signal value convention**: a view or modifier holds **one `Signal<T>`
   field** for a reactive value — never a raw field *plus* a signal field for the
   same value. Static values are authored through the raw config setter (or the
   `.of(T)` convenience), which
   wraps them in `Signals.constant(...)` (e.g. `Text.make(t -> t.text("Hello"))` ≡
   `Text.make(t -> t.text(Signals.constant("Hello")))`); the emitter treats a
   `ConstantSignal` as
   a plain, non-reactive property (no binding/effect), so statics carry zero
   binding overhead. Controls' config fields for *distinct* properties
   (`min`/`max`/`step`/`placeholder`/`mode`/`style`) stay raw.

 ## Project Vision
 
 **Pathland is a cross-platform, cross-language UI protocol** that enables retained-mode UI development with multiple renderer backends. It is **protocol-first**, meaning the protocol specification is the source of truth, not any particular implementation.
 
 **Primary Goal**: Write once, run anywhere - Enable UI code to be written once and deployed across web, mobile, desktop, and embedded platforms through different renderer implementations.
 
 **Status**: The Rust opcode engine (16-byte opcode, ring buffer, arena, diff-based reactive emission) is implemented and tested (`cargo test`). See the Architecture section above.
 
 ---
 
 ## CRITICAL ARCHITECTURAL PRINCIPLES
 
 ### Principle 1: Renderer Statelessness (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
 
 > **The renderer MUST NOT retain application state.**
 
 - Renderers are **pure functions** of the opcode stream: same opcodes → same output
 - A renderer MAY retain its **rendered-output tree** (id → native element + computed layout) for drawing, hit-testing, and event routing — this is a cache of its own output, not state
 - The renderer MUST NOT retain component property values as business state, application control flow, or anything the application can change without emitting an opcode
 - The application owns the canonical retained UI tree
 - The engine emits **deltas only**; the renderer applies them to its native elements
 
 **Violation of this principle is a bug, not a feature.**
 
 ### Principle 2: Command-Based Protocol (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
 
 > **The protocol transmits tree mutations as a stream of commands, NOT as serialized trees.**
 
 - Each frame is a **batch of delta commands** describing changes
 - Only **actual changes** are transmitted (diff-based reactive emission)
 - Protocol acts like a **VM instruction stream** / ABI
 - Deterministic, linear decoding without schema lookup or reflection
 
 ### Principle 3: Binary Protocol (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
 
 > **The protocol MUST be binary.**
 
 - Open-source, cross-platform binary format
 - Fixed **16-byte instructions** in a ring buffer shared with the host via linear memory
 - Custom instruction-based bytecode, not schema-driven serialization
 - **Both directions are binary**: tree mutations (app → renderer) AND raw-input events (renderer → app) share the same instruction format, so the wire is language- and platform-agnostic

 ### Opcode Format
 
 Every opcode is exactly 16 bytes:
 
 ```
 [Category: u8][Command: u8][Flags: u16][A: u32][B: u32][C: u32]
 ```
 
 See `spec/OPCODE.md` for the full format, ring buffer, arena, and frame lifecycle.
 
 ### Machine-readable protocol manifest
 
 `spec/protocol.tsv` is the target-neutral ID manifest emitted from
 `pathland_core::constants` by `pathland-protocol-manifest` (`cargo run -p
 pathland-protocol-manifest`). It contains only `kind`, `group`, `name`, and
 `value`; each language binding keeps its own representation and validates or
 reads the manifest. There is no Rust→Java source generation.
 
 The JVM mirror is hand-written and checked by
 `pathland-view-core/src/test/java/.../ProtocolManifestTest`: every manifest row
 must match a Java constant, no extra public numeric constants may exist, and
 `ValueTypes.forProperty` must match `property_value_type`. CI regenerates the
 manifest from Rust and fails on drift.
 
 Engine behavior beyond individual opcodes is specified in `spec/ENGINE.md` and
 enforced by shared self-contained frame traces under `spec/engine-traces/`.
 `pathland-engine-golden` emits them from the Rust engine and the JVM
 `EngineTraceTest` compares its encoded frames byte-for-byte.
 
 ### Categories
 
 | Category | Value | Direction | Description |
 |----------|-------|-----------|-------------|
 | TREE | 0x01 | Guest → Host | Node create/delete/insert/remove/move |
 | PARAMETER | 0x02 | Guest → Host | Constraint properties (spacing, padding, …), design tokens |
 | EVENT | 0x03 | Host → Guest | Raw inputs: pointer down/move/up, key down/up |
 | META | 0x04 | Both | Reset, environment, window metadata |

 ### Key Property IDs
 
 **Stack**: SPACING=0x0001, ALIGNMENT=0x0002, CONTENT_MARGINS=0x0005  
 **Text**: TEXT=0x000A, TEXT_ALIGNMENT=0x000C, LINE_LIMIT=0x000B, TRUNCATION_MODE=0x000D

 ### Colors
 
 - Literal colors are **sRGB** with D65 white point, packed as `0xAARRGGBB`
 - A color property may instead carry a `DESIGN_TOKEN` reference to a token path
 - Semantic token resolution and theme adaptation are **renderer-owned**
 
 ### Design Token System
 
 **Core Principle**: Application defines intent, overrides, and the theme.
 Renderer defines visual appearance, behavior, defaults, and interaction states.
 
 - The **application owns the theme**: token overrides (base = **light**, `dark.`-prefixed = **dark**) and token references in style properties. Token refs cover COLOR and non-color values (`Length` for spacing/padding/font size/radius/border/frame; `FontFamily.Token` for STRING) in the Rust and Java DSLs.
 - The **renderer owns** default token values (light + dark, the full Tier-1 catalog), token resolution (including explicit `dark.` = forced dark and parent fallback), effective color-scheme detection, interaction states (hover, pressed, focus, disabled), and theme adaptation
 - `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` identifies tokens by **dot-separated string paths** (e.g. `color.primary`, `space.2`) with the standard value-type encoding — there is no separate numeric tokenId system. A `dark.` prefix selects the dark variant (`dark.color.primary`); a `DESIGN_TOKEN` reference whose path starts with `dark.` forces the dark value in either scheme
 - **Runtime theming**: `META::RESET_THEME` clears every app override; a replacement theme is reset + `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` overrides in one frame. `META::SET_COLOR_SCHEME` forces `platform`/`light`/`dark`. Both are renderer state — no node is re-emitted. Java: `Emitter.replaceTheme`/`setColorScheme` + `PathlandSession.setTheme`/`setColorScheme`; Rust: `Engine::reset_theme`/`set_color_scheme`.
 - An unresolvable token reference leaves the property **unset** (renderer default), never an error or stale value.
 - The protocol MUST NEVER describe hover styles, click styles, visual transitions, conditional styling, or layout tuning for interaction states
 - **Deferred**: applying per-component tokens to native GTK/Qt leaf control chrome; web parent-path fallback.
 
 The HTML renderer's default token values are generated from `design/` (see
 "HTML base design" above). Full details: [Design Token System](./spec/OPCODE.md#design-token-system)
 and the canonical catalog / color-scheme contract in [spec/TOKENS.md](./spec/TOKENS.md).

 ## Implementation Guidelines
 
 ### Adding New Component
 1. Add to `component_type` in `lib/rust/crates/pathland-core/src/constants.rs`
 2. Document in `spec/OPCODE.md`
 3. Implement the component type in `pathland-core` (if it affects the retained tree)
 4. Implement native-element mapping in the target renderer (Goal 3–5)
 5. Update the affected project(s)' `status.md`
 
 ### Adding New Property
 1. Add to the appropriate property module in `constants.rs`
 2. Document in `spec/OPCODE.md`
 3. Handle the value type in `pathland-core`'s diff emission (if a stack/text/size property)
 4. Implement in each renderer's property application
 5. Update the affected project(s)' `status.md`
 
 ### Modifying Protocol
 1. Update `spec/OPCODE.md` first (and `spec/CONFORMANCE.md` vectors)
 2. Update `constants.rs` and `pathland-core` encoding/emitters
 3. Run `cd lib/rust && cargo run -p pathland-protocol-manifest` and commit the
    updated `spec/protocol.tsv`
 4. Update the hand-written JVM protocol constants (the Java manifest test fails
    with the exact missing/stale row otherwise)
 5. If emission behavior changed, run
    `cargo run -p pathland-engine-golden -- --emit` and commit the trace fixtures
 6. Verify backward compatibility; update `pathland-core`/renderers + tests
 7. Update the affected project(s)' `status.md`
 
 ### Changing the Wire Format
 - Bump the wire `version` field in `spec/OPCODE.md` and `pathland-core`'s header (currently 1). Pre-release format changes are acceptable while version stays 1.
 
 ### Keeping implementation status updated (MANDATORY)
 
 **The agent MUST keep the per-project `status.md` files in sync with the code.**
 Whenever you land a protocol or renderer change — a new component/property/
 command/event, a new encoder/decoder, a new widget mapping, a new modifier or
 renderer feature, a test that proves new surface — **update the affected
 project's `status.md`** (Implemented / Not implemented / gaps) in the same
 change. The specs (`spec/`) describe the protocol contract only and MUST NOT
 carry implementation status; status lives in `status.md` next to each
 implementing project.

 ## Common Pitfalls
 
 ### NEVER Do These
 | Anti-Pattern | Why Wrong | Correct |
 |--------------|-----------|---------|
 | Renderer stores application state | Violates statelessness | Application owns the tree |
 | Engine computes layout / emits rects | Violates declarative model | Emit structure + constraints; native elements lay out |
 | Send full trees | Inefficient | Diff-based reactive emission |
 | String property names | Larger payloads | Use numeric IDs |
 | String component names | Larger payloads | Use numeric IDs |
 | Generic RGB | Ambiguous | Explicitly sRGB |
 | Hover styles in protocol | Renderer job | Define in theme |
 | Heap allocation in steady-state emission | Slow | Preallocated snapshot slab + arena |

 ---
 
 ## Pathland Mindset
 
 **Always remember**:
 1. Protocol is King
 2. Renderers are Dumb (execute commands only)
 3. Applications are Smart (generate commands)
 4. Only Changes Matter (transmit mutations / reactive emission)
 5. Binary is Beautiful (efficient, deterministic)
 
 **When in doubt**: Check `spec/OPCODE.md`, the conformance vectors in `spec/CONFORMANCE.md`, and the companion catalogs (`spec/PRIMITIVES.md`, `spec/MODIFIERS.md`, `spec/EVENTS.md`, `spec/LAYOUT.md`), and the reference implementation (`pathland-core`). Ask: "Does this maintain stateless renderers?" "Does this only transmit actual changes?" "Does this describe WHAT the UI is, never WHERE?" "Is this representable as a 16-byte opcode in any language?"

 # Contributing to Pathland
 
 Thanks for your interest in Pathland — an open, cross-platform, cross-language
 UI protocol. This guide covers how to build, test, and contribute.
 
 ## Code of conduct
 
 This project is governed by the [Contributor Covenant](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md). By
 participating you agree to abide by its terms.
 
 ## Security
 
 Found a vulnerability? **Do not open a public issue** — report it privately per
 [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md).
 
 ## Project map
 
 - `lib/rust/` — the Rust workspace: `pathland-core` (protocol), `pathland-engine`
   (emitter/signals), `pathland-view` (DSL), `pathland-core-transport`,
   `pathland-core-capi` (C ABI), `pathland-render-gtk`, `pathland-render-html`,
   `pathland-view-native`, `pathland-render-gtk-demo`.
 - `lib/java/` — the Maven reactor: `pathland-view-core`
   (`dev.pathland.view.core*` + `dev.pathland.view.engine`), `pathland-view`
   (the Java DSL, `dev.pathland.view`), `pathland-view-processor`,
   `pathland-view-kotlin` (`dev.pathland.view.dsl`), `pathland-render-html`,
-  `pathland-state-redis`, `pathland-demo-views`, the Quarkus/Spring demos, and
-  the TypeScript DOM renderer (`lib/typescript`).
+  `pathland-state-redis`, `pathland-demo-views`, the DSL-neutral
+  `pathland-quarkus` extension plus the separate `pathland-quarkus-java` and
+  `pathland-quarkus-kotlin` extensions (each with a deployment module), the
+  Quarkus/Spring demos (including the Kotlin Quarkus demo), and the TypeScript
+  DOM renderer (`lib/typescript`).
 - `spec/` — the protocol contract: `OPCODE.md` (primary), `PRIMITIVES.md`,
   `MODIFIERS.md`, `EVENTS.md`, `CONFORMANCE.md` (golden vectors), `ENGINE.md`
   (retained-tree behavior), `DSL.md` (authoring surface), `protocol.tsv` (the
   target-neutral ID manifest), and `engine-traces/` (shared frame fixtures).
 
 Implementation status per project lives in each crate/module's `status.md`.
 
 ## Prerequisites
 
 - **Rust**: stable toolchain (`rustup`); `wasm32-unknown-unknown` target for the
   `no_std` direction guard.
 - **Java**: JDK 17+ (Maven `release=17`; the whole stack runs on every LTS from 17).
 - **GTK4** (Linux) for `pathland-render-gtk`.
 
 ## Build & test
 
 ```bash
 # Rust workspace
 cd lib/rust && cargo test
 
 # no_std / wasm32 direction guard (requires: rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown)
 cd lib/rust && ./check-wasm.sh
 
 # Regenerate the target-neutral protocol manifest after changing Rust constants
 cd lib/rust && cargo run -p pathland-protocol-manifest
 
 # Regenerate the shared engine trace fixtures after an emission change
 cd lib/rust && cargo run -p pathland-engine-golden -- --emit
 
 # C ABI (cdylib) used by Java JNA / native hosts
 cd lib/rust && cargo build -p pathland-core-capi
 
 # Java reactor (the core libraries; the Quarkus/Spring demos are excluded from
 # CI but buildable with: cd lib/java && mvn -q install)
-cd lib/java && mvn -q -B test -pl '!pathland-quarkus-demo,!pathland-spring-boot-demo'
+cd lib/java && mvn -q -B test -pl '!pathland-quarkus-demo,!pathland-quarkus-kotlin-demo,!pathland-spring-boot-demo'
 ```
 
 CI runs exactly these commands (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`).
 
 ## Making changes
 
 1. Open an issue first (or pick an open one) so the work is visible. Issues are
    labelled by epic: `hardening`, `benchmarking`, `tooling`, `a11y-seo`,
    `packaging`, and grouped into milestones `1 · Hardening & Memory Safety`
    through `5 · Packaging & Grant Readiness`.
 2. Create a focused branch (`fix/…`, `feat/…`, `docs/…`).
 3. Keep changes small and reviewable; add/update tests with every change.
 4. Update the relevant `status.md` file when you land protocol or renderer work
    (the specs describe the contract; implementation status lives in `status.md`).
 5. Keep commits atomic with clear messages (see below). No DCO sign-off is
    required.
 
 ## Commit style
 
 - Short, imperative subject line (`feat(view): …`, `fix(transport): …`,
   `docs(spec): …`, `refactor(…): …`).
 - Follow the repo's existing history as the style guide.
 - Reference the issue where useful (`Fixes #NN`).
 
 ## Protocol changes (important)
 
 - Update `spec/OPCODE.md` **first**, plus the affected companion catalog and the
   golden vectors in `spec/CONFORMANCE.md` **before** implementations depend on
   the change.
 - Keep the 16-byte opcode format stable; wire-format changes must bump the
   `version` field (currently 1) per `spec/OPCODE.md`.
 - New components/properties: allocate IDs in the specs + `constants.rs`
   (`lib/rust/crates/pathland-core/src/constants.rs`), then mirror across
   `lib/java/…/Components.java`/`Properties.java` and `lib/typescript/src/constants.ts`,
   and update each renderer + its `status.md`.
 
 ## Non-negotiable principles
 
 - Renderers are **stateless pure functions** of the opcode stream.
 - The engine emits **structure + constraints**, never positions/rects.
 - Emission is **diff-based**: only changed nodes emit; unchanged trees emit zero
   opcodes.
 - Binary both ways: tree mutations (app → renderer) and raw-input events
   (renderer → app) share the 16-byte opcode format.
 
 ## Communication
 
 - Issues/PRs are the primary channel.
 - Contact the maintainers at `michael@apaq.dk` for private matters.

Declarative UI — written once in any language, rendered natively anywhere. **Status: proof of concept.** It works end to end and the tests are green, but the wire format and APIs may change before 1.0. [![CI](https://github.com/PathlandDev/Pathland/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/PathlandDev/Pathland/actions/workflows/ci.yml) ## Pathland is a protocol Pathland is first and foremost a **binary UI protocol** — not just a framework, and not a single rendering target. Your view declaration compiles to fixed 16-byte opcodes that any renderer applies to native elements. The wire is the contract: a view written in Java, Rust, C#, or anything else produces the **same opcode stream**, and any renderer can apply it. That makes Pathland **language- and renderer-agnostic**: - **Write the UI once, declaratively.** A SwiftUI-shaped DSL in your language of choice — Java, Rust, C#, anything — describes the same view structure, whatever it later runs on. - **Run it on any surface.** The same view code drives today's server-rendered web and the native GTK4 desktop renderer, and is on track for the browser via WASM, embedded chips (LVGL), and native mobile/desktop (SwiftUI/UIKit, Jetpack Compose, Qt) ([Where it's headed](#where-its-headed)). - **Only changes travel.** The protocol is a stream of tiny binary deltas: an unchanged screen transmits zero bytes, and updates are applied in place. **Server-side rendering is the first surface we ship** — the flagship getting-started path — **not the whole story**. It's the on-ramp that's useful today; the protocol underneath is where the portability comes from. ## See it in action The same shared demo views, rendered by two of Pathland's surfaces — server-side HTML in the browser and native GTK4 widgets on the desktop:

Browser — SSR + live WebSocket deltas
Desktop — native GTK4 renderer
Try the hosted Quarkus demo live: **[pathland.onrender.com](https://pathland.onrender.com)**. ## The flagship path today: SSR The fastest way to replace a BFF + JavaScript-frontend stack. You write the **whole UI in your backend language** — Java, C#, Rust, anything. Pathland renders the first page as server-side HTML, so it appears instantly, then keeps it alive with tiny binary updates over a WebSocket. The result is a smooth, reactive UI — delivered by the backend team, without npm, bundlers, an extra build pipeline, or a separate frontend. ``` You declare the UI in your backend │ ▼ The server renders it (HTML) and owns it │ ▼ Only the things that change travel to the client │ ▼ The client applies them to native elements (60FPS) ``` - **You declare the UI** with a SwiftUI-shaped DSL — `VStack`, `Text`, `Button`, styling — right next to your business logic. - **The server renders and owns it.** The first page is plain HTML (instant paint, SEO-friendly); the server keeps the authoritative copy of the UI. - **Only changes travel.** A click, a signal update, a navigation — the server sends a few tiny binary bytes describing exactly what changed. An unchanged screen sends nothing. The client applies them to real native elements (browser DOM, GTK widgets), so the platform does the layout, animation, and accessibility. ## The whole app Add one dependency and one bean, and you have a working app. **Spring Boot** ```java @SpringBootApplication public class MyApp { public static void main(String[] args) { SpringApplication.run(MyApp.class, args); } @Bean PathlandApp pathlandApp() { return () -> new MyHomeView(); } } ``` **Quarkus** ```java @ApplicationScoped public class MyApp implements PathlandApp { public View newRoot() { return new MyHomeView(); } } ``` `MyHomeView` is just Java views — the same code runs on both: ```java public final class MyHomeView implements View { State count = new State<>(0); // persisted per session, automatically @Override public View body() { return VStack.make(v -> v.alignment(HorizontalAlignment.CENTER).spacing(8)) .modifiers(padding(24)) .children( Text.make(Signals.computed(() -> "Clicked " + count.get() + " times")), Button.make(b -> b.title("Click me").action(() -> count.update(v -> v + 1)))); } } ``` That's it — SSR at any path, live updates over `/ws`, per-session state. *(Imports omitted: `dev.pathland.server.PathlandApp`, `dev.pathland.view.*`, and `import static dev.pathland.view.Modifiers.*;` for the modifier function.)* ## What it removes Today's server team pays for a BFF, a client-side state model, a SPA framework, and a JS build toolchain — all to render UI the server already owns. Pathland removes that layer: the backend *is* the application. There is no frontend contract to maintain, no client state model, and no JavaScript to write — and the same backend code that serves the web can drive other renderers later. ## Why it's smooth Pathland is built for smooth 60FPS UIs: - **Only changes are sent.** A screen that isn't changing transmits zero bytes. Updates are tiny binary deltas, not re-rendered pages or JSON trees. - **Native elements, not a canvas.** The platform lays out and animates real elements — you get native layout, text rendering, and accessibility for free, whether those elements are DOM nodes or GTK widgets. - **A thin client.** The web client is a small static file that hydrates the server HTML and applies updates in place. No framework, no virtual DOM, no re-render cost. ## The part you don't write The web client is a single prebuilt JavaScript file you copy into your static resources. It's shipped, not maintained — all the real logic lives in your backend. (There's also a native GTK renderer for desktop.) ## Where it runs today -- **Web (SSR + live WebSocket deltas)** — Java, with Spring Boot and Quarkus - starters and demos; the flagship getting-started path. +- **Web (SSR + live WebSocket deltas)** — Java and Kotlin, with Spring Boot and + Quarkus extensions and demos; the flagship getting-started path. - **Native desktop (GTK4)** — a renderer driven by the same protocol, from both the Rust DSL and the shared Java demo views (`pathland-gtk-demo`). Two surfaces, one protocol — the demos' shared views run under both without a rewrite. ## Where it's headed The SSR path above is the on-ramp — the protocol isn't limited to it. Write the app logic once, run it on embedded, mobile, desktop, and browser. Pathland is an open protocol, so the same code that drives the server-rendered UI today can also run on the device itself: - **In the browser**, the app logic compiles to WASM, writes to a shared buffer, and the main thread is left to rendering alone. - **On embedded devices**, the logic runs on one core while another core renders, with the ring buffer carrying the protocol between them — mapped onto a lightweight UI toolkit like LVGL. - **On mobile and desktop**, the same logic drives native renderers — SwiftUI/UIKit on Apple platforms, Jetpack Compose on Android, Qt and GTK on desktop. Wherever it runs, only tiny binary updates travel across the ring buffer and are applied in place — nothing is re-rendered or serialized, which is what keeps the UI stutter-free, even on small devices. ## Try it Each demo has a one-command launcher in [`scripts/`](./scripts/).  # Releasing Pathland
 
 Publishing a **GitHub Release** (tagged `vX.Y.Z`) runs
 `.github/workflows/release.yml`, which sets the version from the tag, builds and
 publishes every artifact, attaches the built files to the Release, and commits
 the version back to `main`:
 
 | Ecosystem | Artifacts | Registry |
 |-----------|-----------|----------|
 | Rust | `pathland-core`, `pathland-engine`, `pathland-view`, `pathland-core-transport`, `pathland-render-html` | crates.io |
 | Java | `dev.pathland:*` libraries (incl. the renderer's native libs for windows-x86_64, linux-x86_64, linux-aarch64, macos-aarch64) | Maven Central |
 
 ## Versioning (tag-driven)
 
 **The tag drives the version** — no pre-bump commit is needed:
 
 - The workflow writes `X.Y.Z` (from the tag `vX.Y.Z`) into
   `lib/rust/Cargo.toml` (`[workspace.package] version` + the intra-workspace
   path-dep pins, via `cargo set-version --workspace`) and
   `lib/java/pom.xml` (via `mvn versions:set`) **in CI**, then publishes.
 - A `bump` job then commits that version back to `main`, so `main` always
   reflects the latest release.
 
 Tags must be `v<major>.<minor>.<patch>` (an optional pre-release suffix is
 allowed); the `version` job fails on anything else. Releases are immutable per
 version — pick a new tag to re-release.
 
 ## One-time setup
 
 Repository secrets (Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions):
 
 - `CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN` — a crates.io API token with publish scope
   (https://crates.io/settings/tokens).
 - `GPG_PRIVATE_KEY` — an armored GPG private key whose public key is on a
   keyserver (Central verifies the signatures).
 - `GPG_PASSPHRASE` — that key's passphrase.
 - `CENTRAL_USERNAME` / `CENTRAL_PASSWORD` — a Sonatype Central Portal **user
   token** (https://central.sonatype.com/account).
 
 Also: `main` must be pushable by the workflow's `GITHUB_TOKEN` (the `bump` job).
 If `main` is protected, allow the Actions bot, or the bump step fails (after a
 successful publish).
 
 ## Release
 
 1. Create a **GitHub Release** on `main` tagged `vX.Y.Z` (publish it).
 2. The workflow runs:
    - `version` — derive + validate `X.Y.Z` from the tag.
    - `rust` — set the version, test the publishable crates, publish them to
      crates.io in dependency order, upload the `.crate` files.
    - `java-natives` — build `libpathland_render_html` for windows-x86_64,
      linux-x86_64, linux-aarch64, macos-aarch64.
     - `java` — set the version, stage the natives into the renderer jar, run
       `mvn -P release deploy` to Maven Central (auto-published after validation).
     - `bump` — commit the version back to `main`.
     - `release-assets` — attach the `.crate` files, the Java main jars, and the
       four native libs to the GitHub Release.
 
 The Java deploy runs on **Maven 3.9.9** (pinned in the workflow): Maven 3.10
 writes a `maven-metadata-local.xml` beside each artifact in the Central staging,
 which the Portal rejects ("content that does NOT have a .pom file"). The demos
-are **excluded from the release reactor** (`-pl '!pathland-demo-views,!pathland-gtk-demo,!pathland-quarkus-demo,!pathland-spring-boot-demo'`)
+are **excluded from the release reactor** (`-pl '!pathland-demo-views,!pathland-gtk-demo,!pathland-quarkus-demo,!pathland-quarkus-kotlin-demo,!pathland-spring-boot-demo'`)
 — `central-publishing-maven-plugin` bundles every reactor module, ignoring
 `maven.deploy.skip`, and the demos must not be published.
 
 The publish steps are **idempotent**: a crate+version already on crates.io is
 skipped, so re-running a partially failed release is safe (re-run the workflow
 via `workflow_dispatch`, passing the `tag`). Maven Central rejects a re-deploy of
 an existing version, so a Java re-run only helps if the Java deploy did not
 complete.
 
 ## Local pre-flight
 
 Rust — `cargo publish --dry-run -p pathland-core` validates the leaf crate (the
 dependent crates can only be dry-run once their dependencies are on crates.io,
 so the ordered CI publish validates them).
 
 Java — `mvn -P release verify` builds and signs the sources/javadoc jars without
 uploading. It needs GPG installed and a `central` server in `~/.m2/settings.xml`:
 
 ```xml
 <server>
   <id>central</id>
   <username>TOKEN_USERNAME</username>
   <password>TOKEN_PASSWORD</password>
 </server>
 ```
 
 ## Publishable crates (dependency order)
 
 ```
 pathland-core → pathland-engine → pathland-view → pathland-core-transport → pathland-render-html
 ```
 
 (`pathland-view-native`, `pathland-core-capi`, `pathland-render-gtk`,
 `pathland-render-gtk-demo`, `pathland-html-golden`, `pathland-ts-codegen` are
 **not** published — C-ABI cdylibs, the GTK renderer, and dev tools.)
 
 ## Published Java modules
 
-`pathland-view`, `pathland-view-processor`, `pathland-render-html`,
-`pathland-state-redis`, `pathland-server-core`, `pathland-observability`,
-`pathland-test-kit`, `pathland-spring-boot-starter`, `pathland-quarkus-starter`
-(plus the `pathland-parent` POM). The demo modules
+`pathland-view-core`, `pathland-view`, `pathland-view-processor`,

+`pathland-quarkus-kotlin`, `pathland-quarkus-kotlin-deployment`,
+`pathland-quarkus-starter` (plus the `pathland-parent` POM). The demo modules
 (`pathland-demo-views`, `pathland-gtk-demo`, `pathland-quarkus-demo`,
-`pathland-spring-boot-demo`) set `maven.deploy.skip`.

+# pathland-quarkus-java — implementation status
+
+**Last updated:** November 1, 2026
+
+Quarkus extension for the Java authoring DSL. It depends on the DSL-neutral
+`pathland-quarkus` extension and adds `pathland-view`.
+
+## Implemented
+
+- Runtime module `pathland-quarkus-java` + deployment module
+  `pathland-quarkus-java-deployment`.
+- Provides the `dev.pathland.quarkus.java` capability.
+- No server/runtime logic of its own; SSR, WebSocket, sessions, state and assets
+  stay in `pathland-quarkus`.
+- `pathland-quarkus-starter` is a deprecated compatibility alias for this
+  extension.
+
+## Transitional status
+
+The Java DSL remains first-class while the Kotlin DSL becomes the primary JVM
+authoring surface. When the Java DSL is retired, this extension and the starter
+alias can be deleted without touching `pathland-quarkus` or
+`pathland-quarkus-kotlin`.

+package dev.pathland.demo.quarkus.kotlin
+
+import dev.pathland.view.core.FontWeight
+import dev.pathland.view.core.View
+import dev.pathland.view.dsl.Button
+import dev.pathland.view.dsl.ForEach
+import dev.pathland.view.dsl.HStack
+import dev.pathland.view.dsl.KotlinView
+import dev.pathland.view.dsl.Text
+import dev.pathland.view.dsl.TextField
+import dev.pathland.view.dsl.VStack
+import dev.pathland.view.dsl.computed
+import dev.pathland.view.dsl.fontSize
+import dev.pathland.view.dsl.fontWeight
+import dev.pathland.view.dsl.frame
+import dev.pathland.view.dsl.padding
+
+/**
+ * A small Kotlin-owned view that exercises persisted state, two-way text input,
+ * reactive plain-Kotlin control flow, `ForEach`, and the Kotlin modifier sugar.
+ */
+class KotlinDemoView : KotlinView() {
+
+    private var count by state(0)
+    private val name = mutableState("", "demo.name")
+    private var items by state(listOf("First item", "Second item"))
+
+    override fun body(): View = VStack(spacing = 16f) {
+        Text("Pathland Kotlin Demo")
+            .fontSize(28f)
+            .fontWeight(FontWeight.BOLD)
+        Text("SSR plus live 16-byte opcode deltas, authored in Kotlin.")
+
+        HStack(spacing = 12f) {
+            Text("Count: $count")
+            Button("Increment") { count += 1 }
+            Button("Reset") { count = 0 }
+        }
+
+        TextField("Your name", name)
+        Text(computed { "Hello, ${name.value.ifBlank { "world" }}" })
+
+        HStack(spacing = 12f) {
+            Button("Add item") { items = items + "Item ${items.size + 1}" }
+            Button("Clear items") { items = emptyList() }
+        }
+
+        ForEach(items) { item, _ -> Text("• $item") }
+    }.padding(24).frame { maxWidth(720f) }
+}

+package dev.pathland.demo.quarkus.kotlin
+
+import io.quarkus.test.common.http.TestHTTPResource
+import io.quarkus.test.junit.QuarkusTest
+import org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertEquals
+import org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertTrue
+import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test
+import java.net.URI
+import java.net.URL
+import java.net.http.HttpClient
+import java.net.http.HttpRequest
+import java.net.http.HttpResponse
+
+/** The Kotlin app boots, its CDI bean is discovered, and SSR renders the Kotlin tree. */
+@QuarkusTest
+class KotlinDemoSmokeTest {
+
+    @TestHTTPResource("/")
+    lateinit var base: URL
+
+    @Test
+    fun ssrRendersTheKotlinDemo() {
+        val response = HttpClient.newHttpClient().send(
+            HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create(base.toString())).GET().build(),
+            HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString(),
+        )
+
+        assertEquals(200, response.statusCode())
+        assertTrue(response.body().contains("Pathland Kotlin Demo"), response.body())
+        assertTrue(response.body().contains("Count: 0"), response.body())
+        assertTrue(response.body().contains("First item"), response.body())
+    }
+}

+# pathland-quarkus-kotlin-demo — implementation status
+
+**Last updated:** November 1, 2026
+
+Kotlin-first Quarkus demo: SSR plus live 16-byte opcode deltas over WebSocket,
+authored with `pathland-view-kotlin` and hosted by `pathland-quarkus-kotlin`.
+
+## Implemented
+
+- Kotlin `PathlandApp` CDI bean (`KotlinDemoApplication`) and a Kotlin-owned
+  `KotlinView` root (`KotlinDemoView`).
+- Exercises persisted state (`count`, `items`), two-way text input (`name`),
+  reactive computed text, `ForEach`, and Kotlin modifier sugar.
+- Quarkus Kotlin build setup: `kotlin-maven-plugin`, `all-open` for CDI/JAX-RS
+  annotations, `jvmTarget=17`.
+- Maven Enforcer bans `pathland-view` and `pathland-demo-views`: the demo is
+  Kotlin-DSL-only.
+- `KotlinDemoSmokeTest` (`@QuarkusTest`) asserts the CDI bean is discovered and
+  SSR renders the Kotlin tree.
+- The DOM renderer bundle + service worker are copied by
+  `lib/typescript/scripts/copy-to-demos.mjs`.
+- Run with `scripts/run-quarkus-kotlin-demo.sh` → `http://localhost:8080`.
+
+## Not implemented / gaps
+
+- No WebSocket delta integration test yet; SSR discovery is covered.
+- No Quarkus codestart yet.
+- Native image is not supported (Rust HTML renderer via JNA).

+# pathland-quarkus-kotlin — implementation status
+
+**Last updated:** November 1, 2026
+
+Quarkus extension for the Kotlin authoring DSL. It depends on the DSL-neutral
+`pathland-quarkus` extension, `pathland-view-kotlin`, and `quarkus-kotlin`.
+
+## Implemented
+
+- Runtime module `pathland-quarkus-kotlin` + deployment module
+  `pathland-quarkus-kotlin-deployment`.
+- Provides the `dev.pathland.quarkus.kotlin` capability.
+- No server/runtime logic of its own; SSR, WebSocket, sessions, state and assets
+  stay in `pathland-quarkus`.
+- **No Java DSL dependency**: Maven Enforcer bans `pathland-view` and
+  `pathland-demo-views` from the dependency tree.
+
+## Build contract
+
+The extension can enable Quarkus Kotlin support, but it cannot add a Kotlin
+compiler plugin to an application. Kotlin apps must configure
+`kotlin-maven-plugin` (or the Gradle Kotlin plugin), including `all-open` for
+CDI/JAX-RS annotations. The Kotlin demo and (later) the codestart carry that
+configuration.
+
+## Not implemented / gaps
+
+- No Quarkus codestart yet.
+- Native image is not supported; the Rust HTML renderer is loaded through JNA.

 # pathland-view-core (JVM engine) — implementation status
 
 **Last updated:** November 1, 2026
 
 The shared, framework-agnostic JVM engine and runtime for the Pathland protocol.
 It owns the `View` SPI and shared authoring vocabulary, the retained-tree
 diff emitter, signals/computed/effects, the wire codec, router, cross-platform
 state, and JNA ring interop. The Java DSL (`pathland-view`) and the Kotlin DSL
 (`pathland-view-kotlin`) are authoring layers over this module; server and
 renderer modules depend on core only.
 
 ## Implemented
 
 - **Protocol** (`dev.pathland.view.core.protocol`): `Components`, `Properties`,
   `Commands`, `Categories`, `ValueTypes`, `Opcode`, `ValueEncoder`, `WireValue`,
   `TokenPath`.
 - **Signals** (`dev.pathland.view.core.signal`): `signal`/`computed`/`effect`/
   `untracked`, synchronous glitch-free flush, equality suppression, error
   caching/retry, circular-dependency detection, and a thread-safe global
   `Scheduler`.
 - **State** (`dev.pathland.view.core.state`): `State`/`PersistentState`,
-  untyped `StateStore`, in-memory store and provider.
+  untyped `StateStore`, in-memory store and provider. Generated
+  `<View>_StateBinder` classes are loaded from the view's own classloader, so
+  application views keep working when a host loads the core in a parent
+  extension classloader (Quarkus).
 - **Transport** (`dev.pathland.view.core.transport`): `ProtocolFrame`,
   `FrameCodec`, `Event`, `EnvironmentData`, `OpcodeSink`, `FrameOpcodeSink`.
 - **Router** (`dev.pathland.view.core.router`): `Route`, `RouteTable`, `Router`,
   `Navigation`, `NavigationContainer`, `NavigationIntent`, `Params`, `Chrome`,
   `NavOp`. `NavigationLink` stays in the Java DSL because it composes `Button`.
 - **JNA interop** (`dev.pathland.view.core.ffm`): lazy `PathlandCore` binding and
   `RingOpcodeSink` over `libpathland_core`.
 - **Emitter** (`dev.pathland.view.engine`): `Emitter`, `PathlandNode`, `ViewSlot`,
   `RenderResult`, `InputDispatcher`, `ReactiveValues`, `DateInput`, `MediaInput`.
   Implements mount/id assignment, diff-based reactive emission, node-level binding
   effects, structural reconciliation, fit/media/navigation routing, and the
   zero-opcode unchanged recompute contract.
 - **Shared SPI/values** (`dev.pathland.view.core`): `View`, `ViewModifier`,
   `Configurable`, `ChildrenView`, `Modified`, `ViewBuilder`, `Configurators`,
   `Environment*`, `Platform`, `Theme*`, `MediaController`, `WindowMetadata`,
   `ProxyConfig`, `Color`, `Length`, shared enums, style protocols, and modifier
   wrappers.
 - **Protocol manifest validation** (`ProtocolManifestTest`): the hand-written
   protocol constants (`Components`, `Properties`, `Commands`, `Categories`,
   `ValueTypes`) are checked against `spec/protocol.tsv` — including no extra
   public numeric constants and the full `ValueTypes.forProperty` mapping. No
   Java source is generated.
 - **Shared engine traces**: `EngineTraceTest` (in `pathland-view`) runs the
   mount/text/property scenarios against the Rust-emitted PLPL fixtures under
   `spec/engine-traces/`, byte-for-byte. The canonical order lives in
   `spec/ENGINE.md`.
 - **Test coverage**: the Java DSL module's test suite exercises the engine
   end-to-end (emitter/reconcile, signals, state, router, transport, JNA ring),
   plus the server/HTML/desktop consumers.
 
 ## Package boundary
 
 - `pathland-view-core` is one Maven module for now: `core`/`engine` are logical
   subpackages inside it, with a few deliberate intra-module references
   (`Color`/`MediaController`/`Modified` materialize `PathlandNode`). Splitting
   `core` and `engine` into separate artifacts requires a node SPI first.
 - Production runtimes/renderers (`pathland-server-core`,
   `pathland-render-html`, `pathland-state-redis`, `pathland-test-kit`) depend on
   core, not on the Java DSL. Tests that author views through the DSL add
   `pathland-view` in test scope. The app-facing starters do depend on
   `pathland-view` because application code authors its root `View` with the DSL.

 # @pathland/dom-renderer
 
 The **Pathland DOM renderer** — the web client. A small, vanilla-TypeScript
 hydration client (zero runtime dependencies) that:
 
 - **Hydrates** the server-rendered DOM by `data-pathland-id`.
 - **Decodes** self-contained `PLPL` opcode batches (bounds-checked) and applies
   them in place: **`STYLE` deltas** (the full property catalog — layout, text,
   styling, effects, semantic/control variants, plus `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` →
   CSS variables) and **`TREE` deltas** (create/delete/insert/remove/move —
   runtime structural updates without a full reload).
 - **Reports raw inputs** back over WebSocket as `EVENT` batches — the full event
   catalog (pointer down/move/up, key down/up, value/text/date changed, focus/
   editing, submit, scroll, wheel) — guest → host (flags `0x0000`), gated by the
   SSR `EVENT_LISTENERS` mask.
 - **Negotiates** the protocol version (mismatch → reload) and **reconnects**
   with exponential backoff.
 
 Styling is renderer-owned: the protocol stays renderer-agnostic. The SSR HTML
 carries a Tailwind-derived preflight plus a tokenized built-in design system
 (`--pl-*` CSS variables); per-node values are inline style, with literal colors
 inline and semantic design tokens as CSS variables. Native browser controls
 inherit the same preflight + design tokens through `.pathland-*` classes. The
 DOM renderer owns the bounded property → style map (`src/classes.ts`).
 
 ## Layout
 
 ```
 src/
   constants.ts   protocol constants (mirror spec/)
   plpl.ts        bounds-checked batch parse + string decode
   format.ts      f32/ARGB/date/float formatting
   elements.ts    component → DOM shell factory (TREE create)
   classes.ts     Option A style/state appliers (inline style + ARIA + CSS vars)
   apply.ts       delta application (STYLE + TREE) over the id → Node registry
   events.ts      guest → host EVENT encoders
   transport.ts   WebSocket connect/reconnect/version negotiation
   index.ts       bootstrap (hydrate + connect + listeners)
 ```
 
 ## Build & test
 
 ```bash
 npm ci
 npm test          # vitest (happy-dom): codec round-trips, TREE/STYLE apply, transport
 npm run build     # tsc --noEmit + esbuild -> dist/pathland-dom-renderer.js (IIFE, minified)
-npm run copy-to-demos   # copy the bundle into both Java demos' static dirs
+npm run copy-to-demos   # copy the bundle into the Java demos' static dirs
 ```
 
 The per-window-id service worker has a real-browser E2E (Chromium + WebKit) — the
 worker-engine differences (e.g. WebKit reporting an empty `clientId` on navigations)
 are invisible to jsdom, so they are guarded here:
 
 ```bash
 npx playwright install chromium webkit   # one-time
 npm run test:e2e                          # boots a fixture server + the shipped sw.js
 ```
 
 ## The bundle
 
-`dist/pathland-dom-renderer.js` is served by the Spring Boot and Quarkus demos under a
+`dist/pathland-dom-renderer.js` is served by the Spring Boot and Quarkus (Java + Kotlin) demos under a
 content-hashed name — `dom-renderer-<sha256>.js` (copied into each demo's static
 resources by `npm run copy-to-demos`, which also prunes stale copies and writes the
 `dom-renderer.current` pointer manifest the SSR layer reads to emit the `<script src>`).
 The fresh URL per build busts the immutable asset cache.
 
 ## Transport resilience
 
 `src/transport.ts` reconnects with exponential backoff, keeps the connection
 alive with a `META::PING`/`PONG` heartbeat + no-activity watchdog, and recovers
 from lost deltas: a **sequence gap** (a batch whose per-stream `sequence` breaks
 the chain) makes the client skip the gapped batch and request a full snapshot
 (`META::RESYNC`). See `spec/OPCODE.md` §Transport heartbeat and §Sequence gap
 detection.

 #!/usr/bin/env bash
 # Shared helpers for the Pathland demo scripts. Source this file; it defines
 # $ROOT (the repository root) and the prerequisite-build helpers each demo uses.
 
 ROOT="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.." && pwd)"
 
 # Build the generated HTML base design and sync it into the renderer crate.
 build_design() {
   if [[ ! -d "$ROOT/design/node_modules" ]]; then
     (cd "$ROOT/design" && npm ci)
   fi
   (cd "$ROOT/design" && npm run build)
   "$ROOT/scripts/sync-design-css.sh"
 }
 
 # Build the Rust HTML renderer cdylib (embedded in the Java pathland-render-html jar).
 build_rust_html() {
   build_design
   (cd "$ROOT/lib/rust" && cargo build -p pathland-render-html)
 }
 
 # Build the Rust dylibs the desktop demos link: the core ring (libpathland_core)
 # and the GTK4 renderer (libpathland_gtk).
 build_gtk_dylibs() {
   (cd "$ROOT/lib/rust" && cargo build -p pathland-core-capi -p pathland-render-gtk)
 }
 
 # Build the Rust dylibs the Qt desktop demo links: the core ring
 # (libpathland_core) and the Qt Quick renderer (libpathland_qt).
 build_qt_dylibs() {
   (cd "$ROOT/lib/rust" && cargo build -p pathland-core-capi -p pathland-render-qt)
 }

input.content:
# pathland-quarkus-java — implementation status

**Last updated:** November 1, 2026

Quarkus extension for the Java authoring DSL. It depends on the DSL-neutral
`pathland-quarkus` extension and adds `pathland-view`.

## Implemented

- Runtime module `pathland-quarkus-java` + deployment module
  `pathland-quarkus-java-deployment`.
- Provides the `dev.pathland.quarkus.java` capability.
- No server/runtime logic of its own; SSR, WebSocket, sessions, state and assets
  stay in `pathland-quarkus`.
- `pathland-quarkus-starter` is a deprecated compatibility alias for this
  extension.

## Transitional status

The Java DSL remains first-class while the Kotlin DSL becomes the primary JVM
authoring surface. When the Java DSL is retired, this extension and the starter
alias can be deleted without touching `pathland-quarkus` or
`pathland-quarkus-kotlin`.

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"
         xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 https://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

    <parent>
        <groupId>dev.pathland</groupId>
        <artifactId>pathland-parent</artifactId>
        <version>0.1.5</version>
    </parent>

    <artifactId>pathland-quarkus-kotlin</artifactId>
    <packaging>jar</packaging>

    <name>Pathland Quarkus - Kotlin DSL</name>
    <description>
        Kotlin authoring DSL extension for Pathland on Quarkus. Depends on the DSL-neutral
        pathland-quarkus extension and adds pathland-view-kotlin + Quarkus Kotlin support.
        It deliberately has no dependency on the Java DSL.
    </description>

    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>dev.pathland</groupId>
            <artifactId>pathland-quarkus</artifactId>
            <version>${project.version}</version>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>dev.pathland</groupId>
            <artifactId>pathland-view-kotlin</artifactId>
            <version>${project.version}</version>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>io.quarkus</groupId>
            <artifactId>quarkus-kotlin</artifactId>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>

    <build>
        <plugins>
            <plugin>
                <groupId>io.quarkus</groupId>
                <artifactId>quarkus-extension-maven-plugin</artifactId>
                <executions>
                    <execution>
                        <goals>
                            <goal>extension-descriptor</goal>
                        </goals>
                    </execution>
                </executions>
                <configuration>
                    <capabilities>
                        <provides>dev.pathland.quarkus.kotlin</provides>
                    </capabilities>
                </configuration>
            </plugin>
            <plugin>

input.content:
# pathland-quarkus-kotlin — implementation status

**Last updated:** November 1, 2026

Quarkus extension for the Kotlin authoring DSL. It depends on the DSL-neutral
`pathland-quarkus` extension, `pathland-view-kotlin`, and `quarkus-kotlin`.

## Implemented

- Runtime module `pathland-quarkus-kotlin` + deployment module
  `pathland-quarkus-kotlin-deployment`.
- Provides the `dev.pathland.quarkus.kotlin` capability.
- No server/runtime logic of its own; SSR, WebSocket, sessions, state and assets
  stay in `pathland-quarkus`.
- **No Java DSL dependency**: Maven Enforcer bans `pathland-view` and
  `pathland-demo-views` from the dependency tree.

## Build contract

The extension can enable Quarkus Kotlin support, but it cannot add a Kotlin
compiler plugin to an application. Kotlin apps must configure
`kotlin-maven-plugin` (or the Gradle Kotlin plugin), including `all-open` for
CDI/JAX-RS annotations. The Kotlin demo and (later) the codestart carry that
configuration.

## Not implemented / gaps

- No Quarkus codestart yet.
- Native image is not supported; the Rust HTML renderer is loaded through JNA.

## What the Pathland extension can do

A Pathland **Kotlin extension** can depend on `io.quarkus:quarkus-kotlin`:

```xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>io.quarkus</groupId>
  <artifactId>quarkus-kotlin</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

Quarkus resolves the runtime and deployment modules of transitive extension dependencies, so adding the Pathland Kotlin extension would make Kotlin’s Quarkus runtime/live-reload support available without the app separately adding `quarkus-kotlin`.

Recommended shape:

```text
pathland-quarkus/                 # core extension, Java-neutral
pathland-quarkus-kotlin/          # optional Kotlin extension
  runtime/    -> pathland-quarkus + pathland-view-kotlin + quarkus-kotlin
  deployment/ -> runtime + quarkus-kotlin-deployment
```

Keep Kotlin out of the core `pathland-quarkus` extension so Java-only Pathland apps do not pull Kotlin/stdlib/reflect unnecessarily.

## What it cannot do

A Quarkus extension **cannot add the Kotlin compiler plugin to the application’s Maven or Gradle build**.

Even with the extension, a Kotlin app still needs:

- `kotlin-maven-plugin` or the Gradle Kotlin plugin
- Kotlin source directories
- the Kotlin `all-open` setup for CDI/`@ApplicationScoped` classes
- a Kotlin compiler version compatible with the Quarkus BOM’s Kotlin libraries

So the correct promise is:

> “Add the Pathland Kotlin extension and get Pathland + Quarkus Kotlin runtime support. Your build still needs Kotlin compilation configured.”

For new projects, a Quarkus **codestart** can generate the Kotlin POM/Gradle setup. That is the right place to solve the build-plugin problem.

## Recommended implementation

1. **Demo first**
   - Add `quarkus-kotlin`, `pathland-view-kotlin`, and `pathland-quarkus-starter`.
   - Configure `kotlin-maven-plugin` and `all-open`.

### [](#kotlin-coroutines-and-mutiny)Kotlin coroutines and Mutiny

Kotlin coroutines provide an imperative programming model that actually gets executed in an asynchronous, reactive manner. To simplify the interoperability between Mutiny and Kotlin there is the module `io.smallrye.reactive:mutiny-kotlin`, described [here](https://smallrye.io/smallrye-mutiny/latest/guides/kotlin/).

## [](#cdi-inject-with-kotlin)CDI @Inject with Kotlin

Kotlin reflection annotation processing differs from Java. You may experience an error when using CDI @Inject such as: "kotlin.UninitializedPropertyAccessException: lateinit property xxx has not been initialized"

In the example below, this can be easily solved by adapting the annotation, adding @field: Default, to handle the lack of a @Target on the Kotlin reflection annotation definition.

```kotlin
import jakarta.inject.Inject
import jakarta.enterprise.inject.Default
import jakarta.enterprise.context.ApplicationScoped

import jakarta.ws.rs.GET
import jakarta.ws.rs.Path
import jakarta.ws.rs.Produces
import jakarta.ws.rs.core.MediaType



@ApplicationScoped
class GreetingService {

    fun greeting(name: String): String {
        return "hello $name"
    }

}

@Path("/")
class ReactiveGreetingResource {

    @Inject
    @field: Default (1)
    lateinit var service: GreetingService

    @GET
    @Produces(MediaType.TEXT_PLAIN)
    @Path("/hello/{name}")
    fun greeting(name: String): String {
        return service.greeting(name)
    }

}
```

**1**

Kotlin requires a @field: xxx qualifier as it has no @Target on the annotation definition. Add @field: xxx in this example. @Default is used as the qualifier, explicitly specifying the use of the default bean.

Alternatively, prefer the use of constructor injection which works without modification of the Java examples, increases testability and complies best to a Kotlin programming style.

```kotlin
import jakarta.enterprise.context.ApplicationScoped

import jakarta.ws.rs.GET
import jakarta.ws.rs.Path
import jakarta.ws.rs.Produces
import jakarta.ws.rs.core.MediaType

@ApplicationScoped
class GreetingService {
    fun greeting(name: String): String {
        return "hello $name"
    }
}

@Path("/")
class ReactiveGreetingResource(
    private val service: GreetingService
) {

    @GET
    @Produces(MediaType.TEXT_PLAIN)
    @Path("/hello/{name}")
    fun greeting(name: String): String {
        return service.greeting(name)
    }

}

## What the Pathland extension can do

A Pathland **Kotlin extension** can depend on `io.quarkus:quarkus-kotlin`:

```xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>io.quarkus</groupId>
  <artifactId>quarkus-kotlin</artifactId>
</dependency>

Recommended shape:

```text
pathland-quarkus/                 # core extension, Java-neutral
pathland-quarkus-kotlin/          # optional Kotlin extension
  runtime/    -> pathland-quarkus + pathland-view-kotlin + quarkus-kotlin
  deployment/ -> runtime + quarkus-kotlin-deployment
